cells.tense: You are at the finish of something and the thinking is still sharp.
cells.act: start something for the spark of starting
cells.ask: Begin the rough version of something that isn't settled — this week, no plan, before the shape shows itself.
cells.core:
The reasoning is quick these days and it's landing somewhere — a conclusion mostly arrived at, work that simply comes together. The endurance under it is quiet and not rigid; you can bear weight without going hard. That's why the thinking can stay fast without fraying at the edges. Something built has reached the point of being usable, and it's being used.

What that usually asks for next is a fresh start, and speed like this is easy to spend only on finishing. So begin the rough version of something that isn't settled — this week, no plan, before the shape shows itself. The shine that belongs after development only appears once a thing leaves your hands, and starting is what tells you what's actually ready.

cells.verb: cutting through to the logic under things, fast

cells.tense: You are pushing to have the analysis finished before the situation has even happened.
cells.act: set a boundary and hold it
cells.ask: Name the hour today when the solving stops — the work, the arguing, the rehearsing — and hold to it even with the question open.
cells.core:
You are working out problems before the moment they arrive, running the argument to its end in your head before the meeting starts. The endurance is holding all of it — you can bear the weight — but the load has grown past what the day actually contains. So you brace for a version of things that hasn't happened, and the reasoning starts advising an event that doesn't exist yet. People can feel the machine running.

There's a plain use of strength here, and it isn't more analysis. Put one firm edge on the day and keep it: the solving stops at a set hour, even with the question open. Whatever you settle on should make sense to others when you say it, since the whole point is a shape that organizes what it touches. A limit that holds does more than one more conclusion does.

cells.tense: You used to hold more than this, and you are still standing where that stopped.
cells.act: teach what you feel by doing it with others
cells.ask: Take some piece of what you understand and do it beside someone who doesn't — same task, your hands and theirs, no explaining first.
cells.core:
The reasoning that used to come fast has slowed or gone quiet, and not much is arriving at the moment. What you could once bear feels heavier than it used to, or you keep tiptoeing around it rather than leaning on it. Clamping down and pushing harder won't fix this; that only meets a tank with nothing in it.

What refills this is company, not effort. Take some piece of what you understand and do it next to someone who doesn't yet: the same task, your hands and theirs, no lecture. Understanding comes back when it's shared with a person, not when it's summoned alone. Pick something small enough that you're both beginners and keep at it beyond one sitting, long enough that the doing, and the truth of what it feels like to do it, passes between you.

cells.tense: The endurance is working, and you are not counting it as yours.
cells.act: ask how it feels to them and stay with the answer
cells.ask: Next time you steady someone, say out loud that you're doing it, then stay a moment longer to hear what it felt like from their side.
cells.core:
There's a steadiness in you that other people lean on — you think it through, you hold the situation up, and when someone asks how you manage it you say anyone would. The quality of it is real and it's doing its work; you just don't put your name to it. It runs in the background the way breathing does.

Naming it takes no more strength than you already spend. When you next steady someone, say out loud that you're doing it, and stay to hear what it felt like from where they stood. You'll hear something about yourself that you can't reason your way to. It lands as recognition rather than a verdict — yours and theirs held at once, which is the plainest thing endurance ever gives you.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim: that the person's speed of thought is currently bearing too much for too long — the draw only shows parsing and speed, not load. The reader's likely objection: 'it's not that I'm worn out, it's that everything else is slow.' The ask survives being wrong: it directs one beat of decision inward, into the person's own next step, not into anyone's perception of them. The sentence that serves the writer more than them: 'You're carrying more than anyone knows' — cut; it flatters the seat rather than describing the mechanism.
